summary: This standards-track document defines an Interactive Voice Response package for the Media Control Channel Framework. It specifies requests to prepare, start, and stop dialog interactions on media connections and conferences, along with responses and notifications. The dialogs themselves are in a separate dialog language.

plainLanguage.summary: A media server is the machine that actually holds the call and plays the audio. An application server is the machine that decides what should happen. This RFC defines the messages those two use to run an automated phone menu: play a recording, collect key presses, record what the caller says, and report back when it is done.

questions: how to control ivr dialogs on media server
what is the mediactrl ivr control package
how does a media server play prompts and collect dtmf
subtitle: A way to tell a media server to run a voice menu: play prompts, collect key presses, record answers.

tldr.problem: An operator's application server needs to drive the media server that holds the call, so it can play an automated menu, collect key presses and record answers, but the Media Control Channel Framework had no defined message set for that.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Control Package called msc-ivr/1.0: XML elements in the urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:msc-ivr namespace, carried in CONTROL and REPORT messages, for preparing, starting and terminating dialogs, for answering requests and for notifying the application server of events.
tldr.outcome: The package also carries a small dialog language of its own, covering prompts, runtime controls, key-press collection and recording, with a status code for every way a request can fail.

today: RFC 6231 is a Proposed Standard and the IANA registry it created was extended by RFC 6623, an IANA registry for the MEDIACTRL Interactive Voice Response control package. The package name, the XML namespace and the media type are the ones registered here, and the framework it builds on is the Media Control Channel Framework in RFC 6230.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Media Control Channel Framework provides a generic approach for the establishment and reporting capabilities of remotely initiated commands. The framework uses many functions provided by the Session Initiation Protocol for the rendezvous and establishment of a reliable channel for control interactions, and introduces the concept of a Control Package. A Control Package is an explicit usage of the control framework for a particular interaction set. This document defines a Control Package for Interactive Voice Response dialogs on media connections and conferences. The term dialog in this document refers to an IVR dialog and is completely unrelated to the notion of a SIP dialog, and the term IVR is used in its inclusive sense, allowing media other than voice for dialog interaction.

The package defines dialog management request elements for preparing, starting and terminating dialog interactions, as well as associated responses and notifications. Dialog interactions are specified using a dialog language, where the language specifies a well-defined syntax and semantics for permitted operations such as playing a prompt or recording input from the user. The package defines a lightweight IVR dialog language supporting prompt playback, runtime controls, DTMF collection and media recording, and allows other dialog languages to be used. These dialog languages are specified inside the dialog management elements for preparing and starting dialog interactions. The package also defines elements for auditing package capabilities and IVR dialogs.

The scope of the lightweight dialog language is playing one or more media resources as a prompt to the user, runtime controls including VCR controls such as speed and volume, collecting DTMF input from the user according to a grammar, and recording user media input. Out of scope are more advanced functions including ASR, TTS, fax, automatic prompt recovery and media transformation. Such functionality can be addressed by other dialog languages such as VoiceXML, by extensions to this package, or by other Control Packages.

The package also aligns with the key concepts of the web model as defined in W3C Voice Browser languages, where the key dialog management mechanism is closely aligned with Call Control XML, and it can largely be seen as a subset of VoiceXML, where basic prompting, DTMF collection and media recording features are incorporated but not the advanced constructs such as forms or a dynamic data model.
sections.plainLanguage: The package covers the everyday phone menu: a recorded greeting, a prompt for a number, a bit of tone control while the recording plays, and capturing the caller's answer. Anything cleverer, such as recognising speech, is left to other languages.

sections.title: How the Package Fits the Framework
sections.content:
The name of this Control Package is msc-ivr/1.0, for Media Server Control, Interactive Voice Response, version 1.0. Since this is the initial version of the package, there are no backwards-compatibility issues to address.

The package specifies control and response messages in terms of XML elements, where the message bodies have the MIME media type application/msc-ivr+xml. These elements describe requests, responses and notifications, and all are contained within a root <mscivr> element.

In this package the media server operates as a Control Server in receiving requests from, and sending responses to, the application server, which operates as the Control Client. Dialog management requests and responses are defined in one part of the document and audit requests and responses in another. Dialog management and audit responses are carried in a framework 200 response or a REPORT message body. The media server also operates as a Control Client when sending event notifications to the application server, which acts as the Control Server; those notifications are carried in CONTROL message bodies, and the application server must respond with a Control Framework 200 response.

The package uses connectionid and conferenceid attributes for various element definitions, and requires that the XML schema for media dialogs and conferences defined in the framework document must be supported. Package responses are different from framework response codes: framework error response codes are used when the request or event notification is invalid, for example a request that is invalid XML (400) or not understood (500).

The package supports auditing of package capabilities and dialogs on the media server. An audit request is carried in a CONTROL message and an audit response in a REPORT message, or a 200 response to the CONTROL if it can execute the audit in time.
sections.plainLanguage: Two roles swap over depending on who is talking. The application server asks the media server to do things and gets answers back; later the media server pushes event notifications to the application server, which acknowledges them.

sections.title: Dialog Management Elements
sections.content:
The dialog management elements are divided into requests, responses and notifications. The request elements sent to the media server are <dialogprepare>, to prepare a dialog for later execution, <dialogstart>, to start a prepared dialog on a connection or conference, and <dialogterminate>, to terminate a dialog.

Responses from the media server describe the status of the requested operation, in a <response> element that includes a mandatory status attribute holding a numeric code. The media server must respond to a request message with a response message, and if it cannot process the request and carry out the operation, it must indicate the class of failure using an appropriate 4xx response code.

Notifications are sent from the media server to provide updates on the status of a dialog or of operations defined within the dialog, in an <event> element. Two event notifications are defined: a DTMF event indicating the DTMF activity, and a dialogexit event indicating that the dialog has exited. If the dialog executed successfully, the dialogexit event includes the information collected during the dialog; if an error occurred during execution, the error information is reported in the dialogexit event. Once a dialogexit event is sent, the dialog lifecycle is terminated.

The <dialogprepare> request asks the media server to retrieve an external dialog document and any external resources it references, and to validate the dialog document syntactically and semantically. A prepared dialog is executed when the media server receives a <dialogstart> request referencing the prepared dialog identifier. The element can carry a source attribute naming an external document, a type attribute naming its MIME media type, the maxage, maxstale and fetchtimeout attributes for HTTP caching and fetching, and a dialogid attribute naming the dialog. The default fetch timeout is 30 seconds. The dialog can be given inline as a <dialog> child element or externally through the source attribute, but not both, and doing both is a syntax error answered with a 400 status code.

The <params> element carries input parameters for dialog languages defined outside this specification. The <param> element inside it names a parameter and its value.
sections.plainLanguage: Three requests, one answer and a stream of events. The media server always answers a request, with a number that says what happened, and it tells the application server when the dialog finishes and what it collected.

sections.title: The Dialog Lifecycle
sections.content:
The document draws the lifecycle of a dialog as a state machine. A dialog starts in the IDLE state. A <dialogprepare> request moves it to PREPARING, and a successful response moves it to PREPARED. A <dialogstart> request moves it to STARTING, and a successful response moves it to STARTED. A <dialogterminate> request, or the end of the dialog itself, moves it to TERMINATED, and a dialogexit notification is sent when that happens.

From PREPARED, a dialogexit notification can also arrive, for example on a timeout, and an error response from any of the preparing or starting steps moves the dialog directly to TERMINATED. In the TERMINATED state the dialog identifier is released, and the media server sends the dialogexit notification carrying whatever the dialog collected in its last execution cycle, or the error that stopped it.
sections.plainLanguage: A dialog has a short life. It is prepared, then started, then it ends. Errors can cut it short at any point, and either way the application server is told when it is over.

sections.title: The Lightweight IVR Dialog Language
sections.content:
An IVR dialog is specified with a <dialog> element. Its attributes are repeatCount, the number of times the dialog is to be executed, where a value of 0 indicates that the dialog is repeated until halted by other means and the default is 1; repeatDur, the maximum duration for dialog execution, with no limit if it is not specified; and repeatUntilComplete, which indicates whether the media server terminates dialog execution when an input operation is completed successfully, defaulting to false. The repeatDur attribute takes priority over repeatCount in determining the maximum duration. When a dialog is repeated more than once, only the results of operations in the last iteration are reported.

The <dialog> element has four possible child elements. The <prompt> element defines media resources to play in sequence, and may itself contain <variable>, <dtmf> and <par> children, and a <media> element naming the resource to play. The <control> element defines how DTMF is used for runtime controls. The <collect> element defines how DTMF is collected, with a <grammar> child naming the grammar to match against. The <record> element defines how recording takes place. The behaviour when both <collect> and <record> are specified is not defined in this package, and a media server that does not support the combination answers with a 433 status code.

The execution model has five steps. If an error occurs during execution, the media server terminates the dialog and reports the error in the dialogexit event. It initialises a counter to zero and starts a duration timer for the value of repeatDur; if the timer expires before the dialog is complete, the dialog is terminated and a dialogexit is sent with status 3. It then initiates a dialog execution cycle, in which each cycle executes the operations associated with the child elements: if a prompt is specified, the prompt playing operation runs and any controls are activated, and if there is no prompt, or when a specified prompt terminates, the collect operation or the record operation starts if the corresponding element is specified. If the cycle completes successfully the counter is incremented, and execution ends when the counter reaches a non-zero repeatCount, or when repeatUntilComplete is true and the collect operation reports a termination status of match or stopped, or the record operation reports stopped, dtmf, maxtime or finalsilence. Otherwise another execution cycle begins.

The exit information elements carry what happened: <promptinfo>, <controlinfo> with a <controlmatch> child, <collectinfo> and <recordinfo> with a <mediainfo> child.
sections.plainLanguage: The dialog is a small script. It can play media, let the caller press keys to control playback, collect key presses against a grammar, and record the caller. The attributes decide how many times it runs and how long it may run for.

sections.title: Response Status Codes
sections.content:
The status codes are used by both the dialog management response and the audit response. The media server must support the status codes defined here, and all other valid but undefined values are reserved for future use. The application server must treat any response it does not recognise as being equivalent to the x00 response code for all classes, so an unrecognised 499 can safely be treated as a 400.

The 4xx failure responses fall into three classes: failure due to a syntax error in the request (400), failure due to an error executing the request on the media server (405 to 419), and failure due to the request requiring a capability not supported by the media server (420 to 439). Where more than one code could apply, the media server should use the most specific code for the detected error: for example 406 when the dialogid in the request is invalid, but 419 when it merely detects that an execution error occurred.

Within the syntax class, 400 means the request is not valid with respect to the XML schema or violates a co-occurrence constraint. In the execution class, 405 means the dialogid is already in use by another dialog, 406 that it does not exist, 407 that the connectionid does not exist, 408 that the conferenceid does not exist, 409 that a referenced external resource could not be retrieved within the timeout interval, 410 that the dialog has been terminated by a dialogterminate request, 411 that the media stream configuration conflicts with itself or with the capabilities of the connection or conference, 412 that a media stream is not available, 413 that control keys with the same value are used, and 419 for any other execution error.

In the unsupported capability class, 420 is an unsupported URI scheme, 421 an unsupported dialog language, 422 an unsupported playback format, 423 an unsupported record format, 424 an unsupported grammar format, 425 an unsupported variable configuration, 426 an unsupported DTMF configuration, 427 an unsupported parameter, 428 an unsupported media stream configuration, 429 an unsupported playback configuration, 430 an unsupported record configuration, 431 an unsupported foreign attribute or element, 432 an attempt to start another dialog on a conference or connection where one is already running, 433 a request containing both collect and record elements that the media server does not support simultaneously, 434 a record element that requires Voice Activity Detection that the media server does not support, 435 an unsupported parallel prompt playback configuration, and 439 any other unsupported capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Every failure has a number. The first digit says what kind of problem it is: 400 for a malformed request, 405 to 419 for something that went wrong while running it, and 420 to 439 for something the media server cannot do at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because this Control Package processes XML markup, implementations must address the security considerations of the XML media type document. They must also address the security, confidentiality and integrity of messages transported over the control channel as described in the framework document, including transport level protection, control channel policy management and session establishment, and of user agent sessions with the media server in both SIP signaling and the associated RTP media flow. Finally, they must address security, confidentiality and integrity of sessions where the media server uploads recordings or retrieves documents and resources.

The document names four concrete risks. An attacker could insert a request into the transport stream and terminate a specific dialog immediately, for example by guessing a dialog identifier that could also be discovered by auditing active dialogs. An attacker could insert new request messages, or modify existing ones, with a very long fetch timeout and a bogus source URL, which will eventually exhaust the connections the media server is able to make. An attacker with access to the control channel could modify the location attribute of a media element to point at different audio, which could then contain a different phone number for callers to ring. And an attacker could modify a record element to add a second recording location, so that the recorded audio is uploaded to the attacker's address as well, without the originator of the request necessarily being aware of the theft.

Because creating dialogs uses media processing resources such as DTMF detectors, playback and recording, the security policy has to address how dialogs are managed across more than one control channel. The identity of a control channel is determined by the channel identifier, the value of the cfw-id attribute in the session description and the Dialog-ID header in the channel protocol. Four policies follow. The media server must only send a response to a dialog management or audit request using the same control channel as the one used to send the request. It must only send notification events for a dialog using the same control channel as it received the request that created the dialog. It must only provide audit information about dialogs created on the same control channel as the one the audit request arrives on. And it should reject requests to audit or manipulate an existing dialog if the channel is not the one used when the dialog was created, answering with a Control Framework 403 response.
sections.plainLanguage: The channel has to be protected, because an attacker on it could kill a dialog, flood the server with fetches, swap the recording played to the caller, or copy the caller's recorded answer to their own address. The package therefore insists that every answer, event and audit result stays on the same channel as the request that caused it.

sections.title: Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has registered a new Media Control Channel Framework Package, a new XML namespace, a new XML schema and a new MIME type, and has created a new registry for IVR prompt variable types.

The package name is msc-ivr/1.0, published in RFC 6231, with the IETF MEDIACTRL working group and Scott McGlashan as contacts. The XML namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:msc-ivr, and the XML schema for it is the one in section 5 of this document.

The MIME media type is application/msc-ivr+xml, with no required parameters and an optional charset parameter whose default is UTF-8. Its intended usage is LIMITED USE, and the applications that use it are implementations of the Media Control Channel Framework IVR package.

The IVR Prompt Variable Type registry is established with three entries: date, time and digits, all for the msc-ivr/1.0 package. A new entry must be published in an RFC and must specify the permitted values of the format attribute and how the value is rendered for each of them, and must not weaken the valid values defined in this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Four things were registered so that the package has a name of its own: the package name, the XML namespace, the schema, and the media type that says the body is XML.

messages.note: A dialogexit event, carrying what the dialog collected.
The application server acknowledges the notification.

transitions.label: dialogexit notification, for example on a timeout

viz.caption: WHAT THE LIGHTWEIGHT DIALOG LANGUAGE CAN DO

items.title: Play prompts
items.text: Play one or more media resources to the user, in document order, optionally with variables in the prompt.

items.title: Runtime controls
items.text: Let the user drive playback with DTMF, including VCR controls such as speed and volume.

items.title: Collect DTMF
items.text: Collect key presses from the user and match them against a grammar.

items.title: Record media
items.text: Record the user's media input, for example to capture a spoken answer.

items.title: Not in this language
items.text: Speech recognition, text to speech, fax, automatic prompt recovery and media transformation are out of scope.

viz.caption: A SELECTION OF THE RESPONSE STATUS CODES

items.label: Syntax error
items.desc: The request is not valid against the XML schema, or breaks a co-occurrence constraint.

items.label: dialogid already exists
items.desc: The requested name is already used by another dialog on the media server.

items.label: Resource cannot be retrieved
items.desc: An external resource could not be fetched within the timeout interval.

items.label: Other execution error
items.desc: The requested operation could not be executed by the media server.

items.label: Unsupported dialog language
items.desc: The request references an external dialog language the media server does not support.

items.label: Unsupported multiple dialog capability
items.desc: The request tries to start another dialog where one is already running.

items.label: Unsupported collect and record capability
items.desc: The request combines collect and record, which the media server does not support at once.

items.label: Other unsupported capability
items.desc: The request needs another capability that the media server does not have.

viz.caption: THE FOUR CHANNEL RULES OF THE PACKAGE

items.title: Responses stay put
items.text: A response goes back only on the control channel that carried the request.

items.title: Notifications stay put
items.text: Event notifications for a dialog go out only on the channel that carried the request that created the dialog.

items.title: Audits stay put
items.text: Audit information is given only about dialogs created on the same control channel as the audit request.

items.title: Rejection
items.text: A request to audit or manipulate a dialog from another channel is refused with a Control Framework 403 response.
